content:
Hi, I'm new here! I'm a compiler engineer, and I was poking around to see if I might be able to make lean go faster, presumably by improving the quality of generated code.

In the limited profiling I've done it seems like there probably is a good amount of overhead that could, in theory, be reduced? I see >10% of time being spent in refcounting, and certainly alloc / dealloc / refcounting dominates the generated code that I've looked at.

As an example, I notice that all (?) functions return a lean_object*, even if the "true" return type is something simple, like a uint8. As a result, callees have to box return types, and callers then have to unbox them. This all also adds additional refcounting overhead. Same for function parameters, which seem to be always (?) lean_object's as well.

In theory (not saying it's easy) you could pass C structs by value for many arguments and return types. Of course this is an ABI change and is therefore only applicable to internal calls. For external calls you could just have a wrapper function that unwraps the arguments and then calls the internal function, then wraps the return object before returning.

Because I'm so new I'm sure I'm missing a lot of context, etc etc. Probably people already have some codegen improvements planned? If so I'd be eager to learn more and maybe help if I can.

Sorry, this part of the code base is not really suitable for contributions from newcomers. It's subtle and difficult to get right. Experienced people are working on it, and our experience so far is that reviewing contributions in these areas is more expensive than doing it ourselves. (Lean FRO employee hat on here!)

Now, there is a path to getting to the point where we believe it's worth reviewing changes from someone here, but it more likely starts with dealing with performance problems and implementation problems with metaprograms in Batteries / Mathlib, and getting some experience there first.
Sure, do you have pointers to the issues you're alluding to?

In the limited profiling I've done it seems like there probably is a good amount of overhead that could, in theory, be reduced? I see >10% of time being spent in refcounting, and certainly alloc / dealloc / refcounting dominates the generated code that I've looked at.

Yes, it is well known that the reference counting creates by far the highest overhead that we have and we have implemented and are still implementing lots of improvements for when and how much we need to perform reference counts.

As an example, I notice that all (?) functions return a lean_object*, even if the "true" return type is something simple, like a uint8. As a result, callees have to box return types, and callers then have to unbox them. This all also adds additional refcounting overhead. Same for function parameters, which seem to be always (?) lean_object's as well.

This is incorrect, the Lean ABI as documented here already prescribes a lot of unboxing that is happening. However, if a function contains an unboxed type in its argument or return type we must also generate a _boxed version of the function for usage in our interpreter and in closures which require a unified ABI. For internal calls we will always use the unboxed variant.

In theory (not saying it's easy) you could pass C structs by value for many arguments and return types. Of course this is an ABI change and is therefore only applicable to internal calls. For external calls you could just have a wrapper function that unwraps the arguments and then calls the internal function, then wraps the return object before returning.

We are aware of this and there are experiments in this direction. However, structure return values under the SystemV ABI proved to have diminishing returns very quickly. For arguments there is a tension between Lean's reset-reuse optimization and unboxing which needs to be investigated properly before going through with such a change.
